title: IBM Links Modular Quantum Fridges Below 15 Millikelvin in Major Step Toward Fault-Tolerant Computing
excerpt: The tech giant connected two box-shaped cryogenic cells at its Poughkeepsie facility, reaching temperatures nearly 200 times colder than deep space as part of its roadmap to a 2029 fault-tolerant quantum computer.
body:
• IBM successfully linked and cooled two modular cryogenic cells to below 15 millikelvin at its Poughkeepsie, New York quantum facility
  • The rectangular cell design provides 12 times more wiring space than IBM Quantum System One and can house at least 2,000 physical qubits per module
  • The milestone feeds directly into IBM's roadmap for its Starling fault-tolerant quantum computer, targeted for 2029

IBM has achieved a critical hardware milestone in its push toward practical quantum computing, successfully connecting and cooling its first modular cryogenic cells to an operating temperature below 15 millikelvin — roughly 200 times colder than the vacuum of deep space.

The demonstration, announced on August 19 at IBM's quantum facility in Poughkeepsie, New York, marks a departure from the traditional cylindrical "chandelier" cryostats that have housed superconducting quantum processors for years. Instead, IBM used rectangular, aluminum-framed cryogenic modules designed to sit tightly side by side, allowing quantum cables to route between them through shared openings protected by multi-layered thermal shielding.

Why Box-Shaped Fridges Matter

The shift from cylindrical to rectangular architecture addresses several long-standing bottlenecks in scaling quantum hardware. Traditional single-chip cryostats impose tight spatial constraints, generate heat bottlenecks, and create qubit crosstalk when thousands of coaxial cables must be routed through a single chamber.

Each of IBM's new modular cells provides 2.75 cubic meters of internal vacuum volume and 0.53 square meters of wiring surface area — yielding up to 12 times more wiring space than IBM Quantum System One fridges, according to the Quantum Computing Report. Each module is engineered to house and cool at least 2,000 physical qubits.

Initial operational tests showed the dual-module assembly cools from room temperature to 4 Kelvin (the liquid helium range) in under five days before reaching the sub-15 millikelvin base temperature required for superconducting qubit operation.

"This new modular architecture uses rectangular units instead of traditional cylindrical cryostats, offering more wiring space and improved thermal management."

— Quantum Computing Report

The Road to Starling

The connected cryogenic cells are a foundational piece of IBM's quantum computing roadmap, which targets a fault-tolerant system called IBM Quantum Starling by 2029.

The architecture enables short interconnect paths between adjacent quantum processing units using IBM's proprietary L-coupler technology. First demonstrated in 2024, L-couplers are meter-scale quantum cables that operate at cryogenic temperatures, enabling direct quantum state transfer and entangling gates between separate physical chips.

Later in 2026, IBM plans to install its Quantum Nighthawk processors into the modular cells for system-level operational testing. By 2027, the company aims to use L-couplers to link multiple processors into a unified system with at least 1,000 programmable qubits — serving as the hardware foundation for Starling.

The Modular Roadmap

IBM's processor roadmap builds incrementally toward the Starling goal. The Quantum Kookaburra processor, expected in 2026, will be IBM's first modular processor designed to store and process encoded information, combining quantum memory with logic operations. The Quantum Cockatoo, planned for 2027, will entangle two Kookaburra modules using L-couplers, linking quantum chips together like nodes in a larger system.

The modular approach avoids the need to manufacture impractically large single chips — a key constraint that has limited quantum processor scaling across the industry.

Industry Context

The announcement arrives amid an acceleration in quantum computing investment globally. Just last week, Bengaluru-based QpiAI inaugurated an 8-inch quantum chip foundry targeting 10,000-qubit processors by 2027, while Tamil Nadu signed MoUs with four quantum technology ventures at the Vetri Conclave. IBM's longtime partner Cisco has also announced plans to build a distributed quantum computing network, linking fault-tolerant systems over long distances.

For the broader tech industry, the demonstration signals that the engineering challenges of scaling quantum systems — particularly the cryogenic infrastructure — are being addressed with concrete hardware rather than theoretical proposals.
